stemBlocks.value: E, C, G and F lie on a circle, EG is a diameter, the tangent AEB at E is parallel to the line CFD, angle AEC = 68° and angle EFD = 106°. Determine, with a reason for each: (i) angle ECD, (ii) angle CEG, (iii) angle CGF.
Think first: Two facts do the work here: a tangent is perpendicular to the diameter through the point of contact, and the tangent–chord angle equals the angle in the alternate segment.

stemBlocks.altText: Source visual for edmar-csec-p244-q10 from workbook page 244.

solutionSteps.instruction: Compare angle AEC with angle ECD using the parallel lines.

contentBlocks.value: AEB is parallel to CD and EC is a transversal, so angle AEC and angle ECD are alternate angles

solutionSteps.instruction: Use the right angle between the tangent and the diameter at E.

contentBlocks.value: ∠AEG = 90° because the tangent AEB is perpendicular to the diameter EG at the point of contact E; then ∠CEG = ∠AEG − ∠AEC = 90 − 68

solutionSteps.instruction: Find angle CGE from the tangent–chord angle at E.

contentBlocks.value: ∠AEC is the angle between the tangent and chord EC, so it equals the angle in the alternate segment, ∠EGC

solutionSteps.instruction: Find angle EGF from angles in the same segment.

contentBlocks.value: ∠EGF and ∠ECF stand on the same chord EF and lie in the same segment, and ∠ECF = ∠ECD = 68° because F lies on CD

solutionSteps.instruction: Add the two angles at G.

strategyBlocks.value: Use the parallel lines to move the 68° from E to C, use the perpendicular tangent to split the 90° at E, and add two equal angles at G to build angle CGF.

finalAnswerBlocks.value: (i) ∠ECD = 68° (alternate angles, AEB parallel to CD)  (ii) ∠CEG = 22° (the tangent is perpendicular to the diameter EG at E, so 90° − 68°)  (iii) ∠CGF = 136° (∠CGE = 68° by the alternate segment theorem and ∠EGF = ∠ECF = 68° as angles in the same segment). The 106° at F is not needed for these three parts.

whyThisWorks.value: The alternate segment theorem links a direction outside the circle (the tangent) with an angle inside it, so the single given 68° can be carried right across the diagram. The parallel line CD repeats that 68° at C, and because angles standing on the same chord from the same side are equal, it reappears at G. Splitting the right angle between tangent and diameter converts the same 68° into the 22° at E.

commonErrors.misconception: Matching the tangent–chord angle with an angle in the wrong segment (the one on the same side as the tangent ray).
